video_title: Why Trend Following Feels Wrong (But Could Boost Your Portfolio)
gist: Turtle trader Jerry Parker (Chesapeake Capital) and Meb Faber argue that 'true' trend following is a strict, low-win-rate/high-payoff subset of the broader 'managed futures' industry, that it should include individual stocks (not just indices), and that most allocators — and even honest quants — are dramatically under-sized in it (Cambria's own unconstrained framework lands near 50% vs. the industry norm of 0-5%), partly because trend is marketed mainly as crash protection instead of its equally important right-tail diversification value.

themes.theme: Trend Following vs. Managed Futures: Definitions Matter

insights.claim: Jerry Parker argues 'managed futures' (the SocGen Trend Index universe) is a broad category that includes mean reversion, carry trades, pattern recognition, short-term trading, and AI-driven strategies — pure trend following is only a subset, now often 50-75% of a typical CTA's book versus 100% for his own funds.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Investors benchmarking or allocating to 'trend' via a generic CTA index may be buying a diluted, multi-strategy product rather than the pure-trend exposure they think they're getting.
insights.quote: It used to be 100% for all the CTAs. Now it's maybe a lot less than that, maybe 50%, 75% for some, 100% for Impute and Chesapeake.

insights.claim: Pure trend-following systems have historically won on only about 40% (or fewer) of trades, relying on the top 5-10% of trades each year to generate essentially all the returns.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: A structurally low batting average is by design, not a red flag — investors evaluating a trend manager on hit rate alone are using the wrong metric.

insights.claim: Meb Faber argues that market-cap-weighted indexing (the S&P 500) is itself a naive, primitive form of trend following: it sizes positions by letting winners grow and losers shrink until they're dropped, and roughly 5% of stocks generate all of the index's gains.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: If investors already accept concentrated, momentum-like return distributions inside their core S&P holding, the philosophical leap to allocating outside it to systematic trend should be smaller than it feels.
insights.quote: 5% of these stocks generate all the gains and just the position sizing algorithm is own more as it goes up less as it goes down until it eventually gets kicked out and that's that.

insights.claim: The key structural difference from indexing: a market-cap index almost never fully exits a stock (it only downweights on the way down and adds on strength, often near tops, as it did with Tesla), whereas systematic trend following has hard entry and exit rules that fully close losing positions.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Passive index holders retain full downside exposure to deteriorating names far longer than a trend-following system would, even though both are 'trend-like' in spirit.

themes.theme: Risk Mechanics: Cut Losses Small, Let Winners Run

insights.claim: Chesapeake caps every losing trade at a small, predetermined stop distance from entry, while deliberately allowing winning trades to give back significant open profit because backtesting shows that capping upside volatility destroys the strategy's ability to capture outliers.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Volatility on winning positions should not be treated as a risk to manage away — for trend systems it is the mechanism that produces the outsized gains that fund all the small losses.
insights.quote: Being concerned with the volatility on winning trades is really something that the back test the computer does not like.

insights.claim: Richard Dennis's original Turtle research methodology was to backtest common trading maxims rather than assume them true — and it showed the popular rule 'never let a profit turn into a loss' is actually a losing constraint for trend systems.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: A widely-repeated risk-management heuristic is empirically wrong for trend strategies — allocators judging a trend manager by how often profits get given back may be penalizing the correct behavior.
insights.quote: One of the worst ideas ever is never let a profit turn into a loss.

insights.claim: Every position at Chesapeake/MFUT, including individual stocks, carries a stop-loss and trailing stop, with re-entry mechanically defined as the next breakout to a new high — removing manager discretion from both exit and re-entry decisions.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Fully rules-based entry/exit is the mechanism that lets the strategy scale across hundreds of uncorrelated markets without manager judgment becoming a bottleneck or a source of behavioral error.

insights.claim: Parker states that trend-following portfolios flip the equity concentration statistic: about 96% of the markets traded end up net-positive contributors, versus buy-and-hold equities where roughly 4% of stocks generate all the index gains and the other 96% barely beat T-bills.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Systematic entry/exit discipline, not stock-picking skill, is what converts a large, diversified universe from a mostly-dead-weight distribution into a mostly-positive one.
insights.quote: 4% of the stocks represent all of the gains for the index and the other 96% don't really beat the Treasury bill rate.

insights.claim: MFUT/Chesapeake uses an equal allocation across the four major sectors — currencies, commodities, stocks, and interest rates — and explicitly avoids overweighting historically better-trending markets or optimizing the portfolio mix, relying instead on 'common sense and a tad of correlation analysis.'
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: The fund is intentionally not curve-fit to the recent past — investors should expect sector weights to stay structurally balanced rather than chase whatever sector trended best last cycle.
insights.quote: MFUD has an equal allocation to currencies and the commodities and the stocks and the interest rates.

insights.claim: Parker deliberately holds highly correlated pairs (crude/Brent, gold/silver, heating oil/crude) rather than picking one, because a single outlier move can appear in only one leg of a correlated pair — citing 1987 when silver doubled or tripled while gold rose only about $20.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Redundant exposure across correlated markets is a deliberate hedge against missing an idiosyncratic outlier, not inefficient overlap.
insights.quote: I think silver doubled or tripled and gold kind of went up 20 bucks.

insights.claim: Position sizing normalizes stop-loss risk to be roughly equal across markets via volatility-based sizing at initiation, but exposures become less uniform once winning trades run and volatility profiles shift — which Parker treats as a feature, not portfolio drift to be corrected.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: A trend portfolio's risk concentration naturally rises during its best periods — investors should not read growing position concentration in winners as a risk-control failure.

insights.claim: Stocks, currencies, and interest rates can each become highly (even near-100%) correlated during shocks; Parker cites April 2025 as a period when the fund lost money 'on everything' because FX and rates positions went fully one-sided across 30-60 contracts each.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Breadth of markets traded does not guarantee diversification during systemic shocks — currencies and rates are more prone to becoming fully one-directional than the far larger stock universe.
insights.quote: we've seen April of 25 where we lost money on everything.

themes.theme: Individual Stocks as an Underused Trend Universe

insights.claim: Chesapeake/MFUT is one of the few trend-following programs that trades individual single stocks rather than only equity indices, arguing that indices mute the very outlier moves (both up and down) that trend following is designed to capture.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: A trend allocator choosing an index-only CTA program is giving up exposure to the single-stock outlier trades that Parker says have recently been among the portfolio's best performers.

insights.claim: Because an index averages many stocks together, a trend system's per-market position-sizing formula can't be applied precisely — Parker frames trading only indices as 'violating' core trend-following mechanics, which single-stock trading restores.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Position-sizing granularity, not just diversification count, is an argument for single-name trend exposure over index-only implementations.

insights.claim: Parker says stocks have been the best-performing trending asset class of the past 10-20 years, and some recent single-stock trades have moved in parabolic, outlier fashion 'like silver or gold or crude' — making equities the sector he says CTAs most under-exploit.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: A CTA that skips single-stock trend exposure is opting out of what Parker calls the strongest-trending sector of the last two decades, likely for AUM/marketing reasons rather than performance logic.

insights.claim: Single-stock futures launched the week of this recording, and Parker signaled Chesapeake would evaluate incorporating them, extending the fund's 'trade any moving market' philosophy beyond exchange-listed equities.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Watch for new single-stock-futures-based trend products; Parker's stated bias is to adopt any instrument that lets the strategy access more outlier moves.
insights.quote: single stock futures just came out on Monday. We'll see where that goes.

insights.claim: Faber notes that broad index returns mask major internal rotation: in 2025 US large caps were up about 10% while small-cap and value indices were up 20-25%, and historically sector leadership fully rotates over time — energy was once roughly a third of the S&P and is now under 5%.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Concentrating on a single headline index (or single country) hides wide dispersion underneath — an argument for breadth of underlying positions over index-level exposure across both equities and geography.
insights.quote: energy, which used to be a third and now is less than 5%.

themes.theme: 'Crisis Alpha' Is Oversold — The Real Diversification Case

insights.claim: Faber argues the managed-futures industry over-markets trend/CTAs purely as 'crisis alpha' (protection when stocks fall 30-50%), which undersells the equally important right-tail benefit of exposure to non-US stocks and real assets that a typical US-stock-heavy portfolio otherwise completely lacks.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Investors should evaluate trend allocations on total diversification value (upside participation in foreign equities, commodities, real assets), not solely on crash-hedge performance.

insights.claim: Parker calls crisis-alpha-optimized CTA products a 'silly situation': some managers deliberately design lower-return strategies to make an easier sales pitch around stock-crash protection, even though allocators still typically cap that allocation at just 5-10%, limiting the real protective benefit anyway.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: A CTA marketed primarily on crisis-alpha framing may be a lower-conviction, worse-performing product than a pure-trend alternative, for a hedge that's sized too small to matter anyway.
insights.quote: it really is a silly situation and I've never subscribed to that.

insights.claim: Faber's diagnostic across advisor portfolios he reviews: the average US advisor runs roughly 80-100% US stocks, has almost no ex-US equity exposure, holds only US and long-duration bonds, and typically has essentially zero real-asset exposure (real estate, TIPS, commodities, commodity equities).
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: These two gaps (no ex-US, no real assets) recur 'almost universally' in the portfolios Cambria reviews — a checklist item for any investor auditing their own allocation.
insights.quote: The average adviser in the US probably has let's call it 80 90 100% in US stocks.

insights.claim: In 2022, when US stocks and bonds fell together, one of the few strategies that actually hedged the portfolio was being short bonds — a position squarely inside trend following's toolkit but outside a standard 60/40 allocator's playbook.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Classic stock/bond diversification can fail simultaneously; a strategy able to go short duration is one of the few mechanisms that hedges that specific joint-drawdown scenario.

insights.claim: Faber's 'lie detector' framing: if forced to size a trend allocation using only historical return and diversification data without bias, he believes every quant and CIO would land near 25%, yet most institutions actually allocate 0-5%, describing a large gap between evidence-based sizing and real-world practice.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: The stated professional consensus (~25% optimal) versus actual allocation (0-5%) implies most institutional books are structurally under-allocated to trend by an order of magnitude relative to their own stated beliefs.
insights.quote: every single quant on the planet, every single CIO would say something like 25%.

insights.claim: Faber discloses that Cambria's own unconstrained strategic-allocation framework has arrived at roughly 50% to trend following, which he describes as likely the largest institutional strategic allocation to trend anywhere.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: This is a direct disclosure of Cambria's own house conviction level — a concrete data point for gauging how far outside consensus the firm is willing to position on trend exposure.
insights.quote: I think in many cases unconstrained, we've arrived at 50%.

insights.claim: Parker argues trend following requires investors to tolerate multi-year stretches of underperformance as the necessary 'price' of eventually capturing outlier returns, framing it as structurally similar to how even top long-term performers like Buffett go through extended underperformance — except at elite pod-shop funds, which he says are exempt.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Allocators should pre-commit to a multi-year underperformance tolerance before investing in trend, since periodic multi-year lag is a feature of the strategy, not a signal to redeem.
insights.quote: trend following is great, but it's not elite. It's not a pod shop thing.

insights.claim: Parker's discipline heuristic: after a 20% loss needing more than 20% to recover feels discouraging, but he calls this merely an 'accounting statement,' not evidence the process or rules have stopped working — trades should be executed identically regardless of how the manager or investor 'feels' about recent performance.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: A behaviorally disciplined investor should judge a systematic strategy on process adherence, not on the psychologically loaded math of drawdown-recovery percentages.

insights.claim: Parker says distinguishing a genuinely 'broken' systematic strategy from a normal drawdown cycle is a real dilemma, referencing an academic (Kenneth French) who reportedly needed a roughly 60-plus-year sample before concluding a factor/strategy had stopped working.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating whether to abandon a validated systematic process after a bad stretch should recognize that statistically meaningful evidence of true strategy failure can require an extremely long sample.

insights.claim: MFUT/Chesapeake was down only about 1-2% in 2025, a mild lag year that followed what Faber called one of the worst roughly-12-month stretches on record for the SocGen Trend Index — both framed as normal variance within trend's expected return pattern, not signs of a broken strategy.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A single-digit lag year after a historically bad prior year is presented as evidence trend is recovering, not deteriorating — relevant context for anyone judging the strategy off recent headline numbers alone.

insights.claim: Parker names gold, silver, and a Japanese yen short as the standout multi-year trend trades of the past couple of years, noting the yen short 'just keeps on giving,' comparable to a Swiss Franc/yen trend trade earlier in his career that lasted five to seven years.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Persistent multi-year trends (like a yen short) can run far longer than intuition suggests, arguing against exiting a trend position on the assumption 'it's gone too far already.'
insights.quote: it's one of those trades that just keeps on giving and keeps going down.

insights.claim: On why nobody sold silver at its highs, Parker says there is no large-sample, backtestable strategy that reliably calls market tops, so trend systems structurally don't attempt to time exact peaks; Faber adds that the same 'obvious in hindsight' top-calling logic would have applied at every prior price level on the way up.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: Investors should not expect (or fault) a trend system for missing exact tops — the same statistical discipline that prevents false top-calls is what allows the system to ride winners to outlier size in the first place.
insights.quote: there is no strategy available with a large sample size that you could back test and confirm that it actually worked that tried to sell silver at those levels.

insights.claim: Cocoa is cited as a market that failed to contribute to trend returns for 15-20 years before one outlier rally flipped it into a net-positive lifetime contributor to the portfolio.
insights.speaker: Jerry Parker
insights.so_what: This is the empirical justification for staying diversified across seemingly 'dead' markets rather than pruning them from a trend portfolio based on recent inactivity.
insights.quote: you get Coco that didn't contribute for 15 or 20 years and then it has this big renaissance and one big outlier changes that to now it's a contributor.
